title: The Ability to Distinguish Big Problems From Small Ones
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that a core, underrated leadership skill is correctly sorting problems by scale, since too many leaders treat every issue as equally urgent and insert themselves into matters better delegated. It gives concrete diagnostic markers for distinguishing Big problems (broad stakeholder impact, high resource demands, time sensitivity, ripple effects into unrelated decisions) from Small ones (contained, straightforward, tolerant of delay). The piece names the underlying temptation directly: leaders feel productive resolving small problems quickly, even though doing so is a poor use of their time and denies others the experience of handling it themselves.
points: Big and Small problems are given distinct, checkable markers — breadth of stakeholder impact, resource intensity, time sensitivity, and ripple effects into unrelated decisions.
The article names the trap explicitly: leaders feel powerful and productive solving small problems quickly, even though it's a poor use of their time.
Delegating small problems is framed as a developmental good for junior staff, not just an efficiency move for the leader.
quotes: For leaders, spending time on problems that others should handle is both a time-wrecker and a morale spoiler.
As a default, too many leaders treat all problems as BIG and insert themselves into issues best delegated to others.

For starters, Big problems are associated with higher risks if left unattended, have a broader impact on multiple stakeholders, and, depending on their solution, have consequences for other decisions currently unconnected to them.
Leaders feel powerful, smart, and action-oriented when they wrestle a Small problem to the ground and resolve it. Unfortunately, it is a horrible use of their time.
Leaders who try to do everything themselves create more problems than they solve.
